📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, said:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very vital to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This noted, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation. The study reveals that lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the de novo protein synthesis needed to consolidate lasting memories, while showing that targeted antioxidants can restore memory function in fruit fly models.

Source: China Medical University.

In a recent development, environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains. Yet despite decades of clinical observation, the precise molecular chain reaction through which lead disrupts memory storage inside individual neurons has remained elusive.

Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.

Published online on November 4, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study demonstrates that lead exposure hijacks mitochondrial redox homeostasis inside memory-consolidation neurons, starving the cell of the newly synthesized proteins required to lock short-term experiences into long-term memory.

To dissect how lead alters neural circuits without the confounding variables of mammalian systemic toxicity, the team turned to the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a premier model organism whose memory-encoding circuits are mapped down to single identified neurons.

Behavioral assays revealed a striking dissociation:.

To observe what occurs inside the brain during memory consolidation, the researchers deployed genetically encoded redox biosensors paired with live fluorescence microscopy.

The imaging pinpointed a pair of dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, cells previously established by Chiang’s group as critical hubs for translating newly synthesized proteins during long-term memory formation. Within these DAL neurons, lead exposure severely disrupted redox homeostasis, tipping mitochondrial oxidation-reduction reactions into acute oxidative stress.

This mitochondrial redox imbalance directly suppressed de novo protein synthesis within the DAL neurons. Without fresh structural and synaptic proteins to remodel neural connections, newly formed memories failed to consolidate.

To verify whether mitochondrial oxidative stress was the primary driver of memory loss, and whether the deficit could be reversed, the investigators administered several antioxidant compounds to lead-exposed flies, including N-acetylcysteine (NAC), astaxanthin, resveratrol, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major catechin found in green tea.

Under controlled experimental conditions, these antioxidants significantly improved long-term memory performance. Deeper cellular imaging confirmed that EGCG reduced mitochondrial oxidative imbalance and restored normal protein synthesis inside the DAL neurons. Furthermore, administering either EGCG or the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO after a period of lead exposure restored the flies’ ability to form latest long-term memories.

According to recent reports, the authors emphasize that while these results demonstrate functional reversibility in fruit flies, they do not show the recovery of previously lost memories, nor do they establish that green tea or over-the-counter supplements can treat human lead poisoning. Further mammalian and clinical studies are necessary to determine whether targeting mitochondrial redox pathways can protect human cognition against heavy metal neurotoxicity.

How does lead exposure specifically affect memory?

Recent findings suggest that in fruit fly experiments, researchers found that lead does not impair immediate learning or short-term memory. Instead, it selectively blocks the consolidation of long-term memories by preventing neurons from manufacturing the new proteins needed to stabilize those memories.

What role do mitochondria play in lead-induced memory loss?

In a recent development, mitochondria regulate cellular energy and oxidation-reduction (redox) balance. Lead causes oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of memory-consolidation neurons (specifically DAL neurons), which shuts down local protein synthesis and prevents long-term memory storage.

Can antioxidants reverse memory damage caused by lead?

In the fruit fly study, antioxidants such as EGCG (found in green tea), NAC, resveratrol, and mitochondria-targeted MitoTEMPO reduced mitochondrial stress, restored neuronal protein synthesis, and allowed lead-exposed flies to form upcoming long-term memories. However, researchers caution that more studies are needed before applying these findings to humans.

Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila.

Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood.

Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms.

Recent findings suggest that using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation.

Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation.

Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

Breaking: How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.
  • In a recent development, unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there.
  • This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

In a recent development, unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

In a recent development, recent global estimates suggest one in five people are currently experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

It has been revealed that despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

Psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

These changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

First, it’s crucial to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

According to recent reports, when that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

One of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”.

While the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

According to recent reports, second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a new diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

Rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

Living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future plans. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

Li-elle Rapaport is a doctoral candidate in clinical psychology and a supervised therapist. Her clinical work is informed by evidence-based approaches, including Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and Mindful Self-Compassion, and her doctoral research focuses on aging and mental health.

Tech Report: What Chimps Can Teach Us About Male Friendships

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value.
  • A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”.
  • But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value. This leaves a large portion of recent generations feeling left behind and forgotten—and vulnerable to exploitation.

A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”.

But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality. Across species—from fungal networks trading nutrients underground to astronauts sharing the role of emptying the latrine on the International Space Station—every organism must strike some balance between competing and cooperating. Lessons from the animal kingdom, from my research and others, show that cooperation doesn’t diminish masculinity.

Indeed, dominant primates use their power judiciously, and male friendship forms the foundation of cooperation in a variety of species, with affectionate touch, caring, and vulnerability playing crucial roles in male relationships. The simple picture painted for these boys is built on sand. Once we observe the reality of sex, behavior, and connection in the natural world around us, it washes away.

Human males stand to improve their relationships, benefit from a broader base of emotional and social support, and enhance their well-being with these friendship lessons from our closest cousins in the animal kingdom.

One term at the core of the manosphere is the notion of alpha males. Life coaches and politicians push this construct without understanding the true function of hierarchy in the natural world. They believe that to get ahead you must take advantage of others, and that the weak get left behind. In reality, dominant male primates care for relationships and wield their power judiciously.

Industry observers note that it’s true that male chimpanzees form typically linear dominance relationships, where one submits to another, all the way to the top. They compete, and those competitions can spill into physical altercations. Higher-ranking males do tend to sire more offspring.

But these broad truths hide the nuance of layered cooperation, care, nurturing touch, and love among male chimps. Day after day, most of that competitive pressure never turns into a fight at all. What holds chimpanzee communities together is less the male at the top and more the alliances underneath him. Males groom each other for hours at a time. They embrace after conflicts and kiss the arms and shoulders of their allies before potential competition, to resolve any tension. Before risky boundary patrols, when they might encounter rival groups, they even hold each other’s genitals—a sign of deep trust. Data spanning nearly three decades from Gombe show that males with strong ties to the alpha sired more offspring than those without, and so did males with wider networks of close allies, whether or not they ever rose in rank at all. Those who look out for each other and contribute to a strong community end up thriving.

You can see the value of those alliances when a hierarchy is disrupted. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, Anna Preis and her colleagues measured urinary cortisol in wild males across stable and unstable dominance periods. Stress rose in every male during the unstable stretches, regardless of rank. Aggression went the other way, rising when things were calm and the group faced less risk of destabilization. When the risk of escalation was greatest, males backed off. Stability has its own payoff; a group tearing itself apart can’t defend a territory.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, even in its origins, the term “alpha” contained more nuance than broadly understood. The term rose out of research during the mid-20th century on captive wolves who were thrown together into crowded spaces without room to escape. Such an arrangement would produce a tense, despotic dynamic in any species, including our own. Once biologists began studying wild wolf packs, it became apparent that they are, well, families. They comprise a breeding pair and their grown offspring. L. David Mech, the biologist who popularized the alpha wolf in the first place, has spent more than two decades asking people to retire the term in order to accurately reflect natural communities. Despite its inaccuracy, the idea still perpetuates on podcasts and social media.

It has been revealed that the role of vulnerability and comfort in the natural world provides another powerful lesson for humanity. At a wildlife sanctuary in Zambia, I’ve come to know a longstanding alpha male chimpanzee named Doug over many years. One day, during my first field season observing his group, he was separated from his community for routine husbandry purposes, alongside a slightly younger rival and the rival’s paternal ally. During this separation, the rival pair ambushed him, leaving him incredibly shaken. I had known Doug as a strong leader who never broke composure, and I felt shocked to see him cowering and screaming, nothing like the composed figurehead his group had respected.

According to recent reports, A low-ranking male, whom Doug had rarely paid attention to, approached first, offering himself in a gesture of submission. What followed drew in most of the roughly 40 other chimpanzees in the group. They embraced, touched, and kissed him; exchanged genital contact; placed their hands in his mouth; and invited him to mount them. This scale of collective reassurance directed toward a single individual is something I’ve never seen since, and is likely only sparked by moments of genuine crisis. The whole group responded to Doug’s distress with an outpouring of comfort and what to humans would appear to be love.

Industry observers note that the main aim of this project was to study consolation: how chimpanzees, and their sister species bonobos, comfort each other after fights. But we kept noticing similar intense, friendly contacts occurring in the absence of conflicts, often in the anticipation of competition. To better understand this, we conducted a feeding task with a five-minute window before the food arrived, filming 116 apes across five groups at two sanctuaries. We found that those who exchanged more reassuring contact beforehand went on to spend significantly more time feeding peacefully alongside others. In chimpanzees, males exhibited most of this behavior, but primarily in Doug’s more tolerant group. In a more despotic group where resources were less evenly distributed, the male-male relationships were markedly weaker. Simply put, friendship and reassuring behaviors among males helped these chimps peacefully put aside competing interests, which may lay the groundwork for collective harmony.

Recent findings suggest that some of these behaviors require remarkable trust. Placing a finger, or even a whole hand, inside another male’s mouth or pressing your own mouth to someone’s body after they’ve just been attacked may be misinterpreted as having aggressive intent and could spark a fresh conflict. Chimpanzees have a reputation for amputating the extremities of others, and that, along with the size of their canines, makes these behaviors exceptionally risky during such turbulent times. Our hypothesis: That could be the point. You only offer that kind of vulnerability to someone you trust not to use it against you, and doing so signals something about the relationship that a show of strength can’t. Again, we noticed that these behaviors were particularly amplified in Doug’s group compared to the one with a less benevolent leader.

Doug remains alpha to this day, and from our research, his tenureship seems to be thanks to the bonds he continues to invest in and the support he shows for his peers. He’s flawed and sometimes lashes out as any male chimpanzee might do, but throughout the seven years we’ve studied him, no challenges have managed to displace him. Doug looks out for others, and in turn they look out for him. Over my time studying many groups of chimpanzees, it seems the most tolerant social environments emerge from the leadership of strong, stable, and generally fair alphas who allow others access to resources and who keep tight bonds with their closest allies.

Industry observers note that humans can also learn from the way male chimpanzees can be tender in other contexts. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, researchers recorded wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned infants, more than half of them taken in by males with no obvious kinship reason to bother. One adult male, Porthos, adopted an unrelated infant female named Gia and carried her on his back for years, sharing food with her long after any potential social debt to her deceased mother had lapsed. Later analysis found that what predicted whether a male took on that role was not the infant’s sex, and not relatedness, but the strength of the grooming bond he’d shared with the mother before she died.

In a recent development, touch carries power in humans, as well. Research across five European cultures found that the area of the body you’ll let someone touch maps almost directly onto the strength of your emotional bond with them. There is cultural variation. British people are notably more guarded about casual contact than many of their European neighbours, and touch between men in many Western contexts carries particular social weight. Touch conveys intimacy and trust. Yet holding someone’s hand or shoulder can also be used to intimidate or harass. We could learn from primates to stop withholding touch where it would help most and back down from reaching for it where it shouldn’t be used at all.

One key area where more touch helps is sports. A study of all 30 NBA teams during the 2008–09 season found that the teams who touched more early in the season, through fist bumps, chest bumps, hugs, and high fives, went on to perform better and play more cooperatively later, even after controlling for player salaries and pre-season expectations. In women’s college basketball, players who received more physical contact from teammates after missing their first free throw were more likely to convert the second. After five straight shootout losses, England’s governing body in football, the FA, spent 18 months rebuilding England’s approach to penalties under Gareth Southgate, not just the technical side. Players were coached on how to treat each other after a miss. They learned to place an arm around the shoulder rather than leaving each other isolated. Celebrating wildly after a scored kick became a deliberate technique for steadying whoever was up next. Locker-room culture has never been shy about physical contact between teammates. Now we know that the contact might be doing real work.

To be sure, humans show exceptional diversity in our cultures and behavior, for better and worse. But when humans are violent or cruel, people call it primal, or animalistic. We emphasize our altruism as unique to our species. That’s unfair to animals. Humans have bullied others until they took their own lives. We’ve wiped out entire tribes and cultures. And beyond targeting other people, even now, humans are removing protections for endangered keystone species that ecosystems depend upon to thrive. But we don’t need to accept the drive to dominate as inevitable. If the apes show anything, it’s how much of that drive gets managed and set aside day to day, and how much depends on the community you find yourself in. We are a part of the natural world like all other animals, needing to balance our cooperative and competitive urges. And the evidence suggests we sit at the better end of that range far more often than we might think.

Now that we know how central touch and cooperation are to primates and human nature, I hope we can stop being pessimistic when we predict others’ behavior and motives. A study published in Science this June, covering 125 countries and over 100,000 people, found that 69% of us cooperate with a stranger when given the choice. Asked to guess, people put it at 47%. That pessimism highlighted up in 124 of the 125 countries surveyed. This matters in the grander scheme of things because those of us who expect others to cooperate are far more likely to cooperate also. When researchers simply told participants that most people worldwide see climate change as a threat, belief in others’ willingness to cooperate ticked up, and actual cooperation followed it, slightly, but in the right direction.

Building on the lessons of primate relationships is easier than it seems.

Seek simple interactions. One of the main ways our primate cousins build affiliative relationships is spending time sitting in close proximity. They may groom, or play, or even sit in contact. More often than not they just like to hang out near their close partners. Just being close to one another is meaningful.

Recent findings suggest that try a car journey or a five-a-side game. Build trust and relationship through activities where nobody has to look anyone in the eye. If a mate isn’t much of a talker, doing something alongside him might get further than sitting him down and asking how he’s doing.

Reach out before a crisis, not after. Great apes exchange most of their reassurance in the tense minutes before competition, not the wreckage afterward. Reconciliation and comforting are commonplace in humans and primates, but it’s much easier to prevent escalation than it is to smooth things over after a fight.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Don’t wait to be the one who’s approached. That 22-point gap between how we actually cooperate and what we think everyone else will do indicates the power of offering an invitation to relationship. Most of us are waiting for someone else to go first.

Influencers selling young men and boys on their primal nature fly in the face of the science and what nature actually looks like. Force and competition are real parts of biology, and something we humans have to manage in our everyday lives. But, if there’s one thing I’ve learned from my many years studying our closest relatives, it’s that touch, care, cooperation, and even love are the most instinctive natural components of being part of the primate family.

Sources indicate that jake Brooker, Ph.D., is an NWO Veni scholar based at Utrecht University, The Netherlands, who studies social cognition and socio-emotional behavior in great apes. He completed doctoral and postdoctoral work at Durham University, U.K.

Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure.
  • Researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy.
  • How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure. Growing evidence suggests that excessive salt intake may also interfere with memory, thinking, and emotional well-being. High salt (HS) consumption is already a major public health concern because of its connection to hypertension, but its potential effects on the brain make finding ways to reduce the damage even more crucial.

Researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy. Previous research found that this ingredient could reduce high blood pressure and cognitive problems associated with a high-salt diet (HSD) in mice. The latest study takes a closer look at how it works, revealing that the compound influences vital chemical signals in the brain and kidneys.

How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt.

According to recent reports, the research centers on prostaglandins (PGs), signaling molecules made from a fatty acid called arachidonic acid (AA). These substances act much like local hormones, helping regulate essential functions throughout the body.

In the cardiovascular system, prostaglandins help control blood pressure by balancing the widening and narrowing of blood vessels. Their effects in the brain are more complicated. Depending on which receptors they activate, they can trigger signals that either protect nerve cells or contribute to harmful processes, potentially affecting memory, thinking, and emotional responses.

LPC70 is a form of soy lysolecithin in which lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) accounts for more than 70% of the phospholipids. Although earlier experiments highlighted that LPC70 could ease salt-related hypertension and cognitive difficulties, scientists had not fully understood the mechanisms responsible, particularly its influence on prostaglandin signaling.

To investigate, a research team led by Professor Akihiro Mouri and Dr. Hisayoshi Kubota, working with Dr. Kazuhiro Kagotani, examined how LPC70 affected these signaling pathways in mice consuming a high-salt diet.

In a recent development, dr. Kubota, the study's first author, played a central role in the experiments. He assessed blood pressure, monitored behavioral changes, and analyzed molecular activity associated with prostaglandins. His work helped clarify how LPC70 produces different effects in the organs involved in salt-related cardiovascular and cognitive problems.

In a recent development, prof. Mouri and Dr. Kubota are affiliated with the Department of Regulatory Science for Evaluation and Development of Pharmaceuticals & Devices at Fujita Health University Graduate School of Medical Science, as well as the International Center for Brain Science (ICBS) at Fujita Health University in Japan. Dr. Kagotani is affiliated with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, in Japan and the Tsuji Health and Beauty Science Laboratory at Mie University, Japan.

The findings were released online on May 14, 2026, and published in Volume 197 of Neurochemistry International on July 1, 2026.

In a recent development, "We wanted to understand the role of LPC70 in coordinating changes in PG signaling across organ systems," mentioned Prof. Mouri. "Our study originated from a collaborative research project with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, a company that develops naturally derived food ingredients," he added.

Soy Compound Improves Blood Pressure and Memory in Mice.

As expected, mice that consumed a high-salt diet developed elevated blood pressure. However, the consequences extended beyond their cardiovascular health.

The animals also became less socially interactive and had difficulty recognizing objects they had encountered before, indicating problems with memory. Interestingly, their general movement and anxiety-like behavior revealed no substantial changes. This pattern suggests that excessive salt selectively disrupted more complex cognitive and social functions rather than causing widespread behavioral impairment.

When researchers supplemented the animals' diets with LPC70, several of these effects were reduced. Blood pressure improved, and the mice performed better on tests of social interaction and object recognition memory.

These improvements prompted the researchers to examine what was happening inside the animals' kidneys and brains.

Different Protective Effects in the Kidneys and Brain.

In the kidneys, a high-salt diet increased the expression of two components involved in prostaglandin signaling: cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and the PGE2 receptor EP3. Both may contribute to the development of high blood pressure associated with excessive salt consumption.

LPC70 reduced these salt-related increases, suggesting that the compound helps correct changes in kidney signaling that can interfere with normal blood pressure regulation.

The researchers found a different response in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region essential for thinking, memory, and social behavior.

Excess salt reduced the expression of the PGD2 receptor DP1, which plays a role in protective and anti-inflammatory signaling in the brain. LPC70 restored expression of this receptor without changing DP2, another receptor associated with potentially harmful effects on nerve cells.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction is vital because it suggests that LPC70 does not simply increase or suppress all prostaglandin activity. Instead, it may selectively favor signaling pathways that help protect the brain, potentially explaining the improvements in memory and social behavior observed in the mice.

A Surprising Change in Chemical Signaling.

The team also discovered an unexpected change involving arachidonic acid, the fatty acid the body uses to produce prostaglandins.

Mice consuming excess salt had lower levels of circulating arachidonic acid. Yet when they received LPC70, levels of prostaglandins derived from this fatty acid, including PGE2 and PGD2, increased.

This seemingly contradictory result suggests that LPC70 may help the body use available arachidonic acid more efficiently to produce prostaglandins under high-salt conditions.

Taken together, the findings reveal a coordinated but highly selective response. In the kidneys, LPC70 appears to suppress signaling changes associated with hypertension. In the brain, it restores signaling linked to protection against inflammation and damage.

The compound's effects therefore depend on both the organ involved and the specific prostaglandin receptors being regulated.

Could Soy-Based Ingredients Help Protect Against Excess Salt?

The results suggest that LPC70 could eventually become a useful functional food ingredient for reducing some of the health consequences of excessive salt intake.

Its ability to improve blood pressure and cognitive performance in mice raises the possibility that it could support cardiovascular and brain health, particularly among people whose diets contain high amounts of salt.

However, the findings come from animal experiments, and further clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same benefits occur in humans.

In a recent development, "Our study elucidates LPC70's role in PG signaling, laying the groundwork for future clinical research and dietary interventions aimed at reducing hypertension-related cognitive decline and promoting healthy aging globally," concluded Prof. Mouri.

The research provides a clearer picture of how a soy-derived compound can influence the body's response to excessive salt, opening new possibilities for nutritional approaches to protecting long-term health.

The study received support through Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS: 20K07931, 22K07606, 22K11891, and 23H02843).

Additional support came from the Fujita Mind-Brain Research & Innovation Center for Drug Generation (Fujita Mind-BRIDGe) through Japan's Peak Research Universities (J-PEAKS) Program (JPJS00420240019), along with the Japan Science and Technology Agency FOREST Program (JPMJFR215H).

Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd. provided funding for the research. Grants and other support were also supplied by the Education and Research Facility of Animal Models for Human Diseases at Fujita Health University, the Smoking Research Foundation, and the Takeda Science Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upcoming research demonstrates that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a systemic condition influencing respiratory patterns, subjective time pressure, brain iron levels, and alcohol use risk across the lifespan. Together, these findings reveal distinct physiological and neural signatures that extend well beyond traditional behavioral symptoms.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

In a recent development, affecting approximately one in nine children in the United States, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions of childhood. While clinical assessments have historically focused on hallmark behavioral traits, inattention, impulsivity, and motor hyperactivity, mounting evidence indicates that ADHD exerts far-reaching effects on physical and mental health well into adulthood.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four newly introduced studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.

Taken together, the emerging findings map distinct physiological and behavioral signatures across development:.

By connecting autonomic physiology, neurochemistry, and lived cognitive stress, these studies challenge narrow definitions of ADHD as purely an attentional or behavioral disorder.

“It is becoming clear that ADHD is a broader systemic condition affecting a host of brain and body variables beyond just motor hyperactivity,” stated press conference moderator Dr. Chandan Vaidya, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University who studies how regulatory behavior goes awry in neurodevelopmental conditions. “Together, these new findings tackle timely topics and showcase the diversity of areas where work is needed to better understand ADHD and ultimately improve diagnosis and treatment.”.

How does ADHD affect physical functions outside of attention and hyperactivity?

New research presented at Neuroscience 2026 reveals that ADHD is linked to distinct breathing patterns in young adults, lower iron levels in specific regions of the developing brain, and chronic psychological time pressure, demonstrating that the condition involves both brain-wide neurochemistry and bodily physiology.

What did researchers discover about brain iron in children with ADHD?

According to recent reports, brain scans conducted by researchers at UC San Diego revealed that children and adolescents with ADHD have lower levels of iron in specific brain regions compared to peers without ADHD. Because iron is crucial for producing neurotransmitters like dopamine, tracking these regional changes may offer upcoming insights into ADHD neurobiology.

Can treating ADHD help reduce alcohol misuse in young adults?

In a recent development, yes. Emerging clinical data from the University of Florida indicates that ADHD medication may help decrease problem drinking behaviors among young adults who experience both ADHD and alcohol use disorder.

17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year.
  • Industry observers note that laura M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Industry observers note that laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together.

Josh (Upcoming Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”.

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories.

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature.

According to recent reports, angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations.

It has been revealed that lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Related GGiE practice: Superstar.

In a recent development, pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a initiative, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students promptly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is notable to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals.

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom).

In a recent development, joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

Related GGiE practice: 1-2-3 Clap.

David (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful.

According to recent reports, susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Related GGiE practice: Truth or Tale.

Industry observers note that harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices.

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”.

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back.

It has been revealed that lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness.

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions.

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a SIGNIFICANT SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome.

According to recent reports, donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity.

Sources indicate that thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the upcoming school year!

We look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

Sarah Bracken is the Director of Education Partnerships at Greater Good Science Center. Prior to joining GGSC, Sarah taught in secondary classrooms from Alaska to Virginia and collaborated with educators to co-create communities of practice and other professional learning opportunities focused on belonging and equitable education for students of refugee and immigrant backgrounds. She is a Nationally Board Certified teacher with a B.A. from the University of Virginia and a Master’s in Teaching from The Evergreen State College.

#10817. Scent and Memory: Why Novelty Boosts Recall in Older Adults

Scent and Memory: Why Novelty Boosts Recall in Older Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults.
  • Industry observers note that the sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus.
  • However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A memory and olfaction study reveals that diffused lavender scent alone does not automatically boost memory performance in young or older adults. unless it is experienced as a novel cue at the very start of learning. The findings show that older adults who encountered the scent during the initial learning block recalled objects significantly better, highlighting how sensory novelty and intact smell function support cognitive aging.

Industry observers note that the sense of smell maintains an unusually direct anatomical highway to the brain’s emotional and memory hubs, bypassing the thalamic relay used by other senses to project straight into the amygdala and hippocampus. Because a single familiar whiff can trigger vivid autobiographical flashbacks, aromatherapy, particularly using lavender essential oil, has frequently been touted as a simple tool to sharpen memory and stave off age-related cognitive decline.

However, rigorous empirical evidence supporting aromatherapy as a universal memory enhancer has remained mixed.

Now, a study published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience by neuroscientists at UCLA and Rice University reveals that the relationship between scent and memory depends heavily on timing, sensory novelty, and baseline olfactory health.

According to recent reports, led by UCLA neuroscientist and corresponding author Dr. Stephanie Leal, the investigation shows that while lavender scent alone did not act as a blanket memory booster, encountering the scent as a fresh, novel stimulus at the beginning of a learning session significantly enhanced recall in older adults.

Because age-related olfactory dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease, Leal and colleagues set out to examine how olfactory cues interact with memory encoding in cognitively healthy younger and older adults.

In a recent development, participants first completed standardized olfactory assessments to measure baseline smell sensitivity before entering either a room diffused with lavender essential oil or an unscented room. Volunteers viewed two sequential blocks of everyday household objects, such as a tomato or a blow dryer, on a computer screen. Crucially, the design was counterbalanced: participants who experienced the lavender scent during the first image block completed the second block in an unscented room, and vice versa.

Following a delay, participants underwent a nuanced memory test featuring images that were either identical to, slightly altered from (e.g., changing a red blow dryer to blue), or completely different from the original items. This paradigm allowed researchers to separate general recall (recognizing the object category) from high-resolution detail memory (remembering exact visual features).

“When we looked at general and detail memory measures, older adults struggled to remember the details, which we expected,” explained Leal. “Interestingly, the presence or absence of odor made no difference for older or younger adults. We were kind of scratching our heads because that was surprising based on prior work that showed olfaction might enhance memory.”.

A deeper look at the experimental order, however, uncovered a striking pattern among older adults:.

These results suggest that as the brain ages, the specific chemical profile of an essential oil matters far less than the novelty of encountering an enriched sensory environment at the onset of learning.

Rather than treating aromatherapy as a passive background cure-all, the findings indicate that olfactory cues work best when deployed strategically to introduce novelty during new learning experiences.

Industry observers note that “If we want to support memory in older adults, we need to think beyond simply whether a stimulus helps or hurts memory and consider when and how it is experienced,” Leal noted. “A big component of learning in aging is novelty. Engaging in learning in an enriched context may make it easier to learn new things.”.

By linking baseline smell sensitivity, subjective pleasantness, and timed sensory novelty to hippocampal memory precision, the research offers practical insights for designing enriched cognitive interventions aimed at supporting healthy brain aging.

Does diffusing lavender essential oil automatically improve memory?

No. Researchers at UCLA and Rice University found that overall, both younger and older adults performed no better on memory tests in a lavender-scented room compared to an unscented room.

Why did encountering the scent first help older adults remember better?

Recent findings suggest that older adults who smelled lavender during the very first learning block recalled objects more accurately than those exposed during the second block. This suggests that the novelty of entering an enriched sensory environment at the start of a task helps the aging brain anchor latest memories.

How does sense of smell connect to Alzheimer’s disease and aging?

Sources indicate that age-related loss of smell is closely linked to early neurodegenerative changes in Alzheimer’s disease. In this study, older adults with healthier baseline olfactory function, and those who found the scent pleasant, highlighted better detail memory, highlighting the close tie between olfactory processing and hippocampal memory circuits.

Funding: The researchers involved in this project were funded by the National Science Foundation, the BrightFocus Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Alzheimer’s Association.

Olfactory context and memory across the adult lifespan: effects on mnemonic discrimination and olfactory function.

Odor is a powerful contextual cue that can influence memory and is closely linked to brain regions involved in episodic memory, including the hippocampus.

According to recent reports, age-related olfactory dysfunction is among the earliest behavioral changes associated with cognitive decline and may contribute to memory impairments in older adults. Hippocampal pattern separation, or the process of reducing interference among similar experiences, provides a sensitive measure of age-related memory decline, yet little is known about how olfactory context influences mnemonic discrimination.

Industry observers note that in the present study, we examined whether odor context during encoding affects subsequent mnemonic discrimination in young and older adults. Participants completed a mnemonic similarity task in which object stimuli were encoded in both odor (lavender) and no-odor contexts prior to a memory test.

Industry observers note that across participants, odor context did not significantly influence target recognition or mnemonic discrimination. Consistent with prior work, older adults exhibited poorer mnemonic discrimination and reduced olfactory function relative to young adults.

Industry observers note that however, odor presentation order influenced mnemonic discrimination in older adults, such that performance was better when the odor context was encountered during the first encoding block compared to the second. Additionally, poorer olfactory function was associated with reduced mnemonic discrimination, and this relationship was largely explained by age-related differences in olfactory ability.

These findings suggest that the influence of olfactory context on memory depends on both age and the timing of odor exposure, highlighting the importance of individual differences in olfactory function when evaluating odor-based approaches to support memory in aging.

How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • Industry observers note that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

Industry observers note that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my proposal and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious prepares produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

In a recent development, repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

According to recent reports, missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a initiative so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

According to recent reports, micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

Industry observers note that I hate the idea of abandoning my significant plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Industry observers note that then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

According to recent reports, do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Sources indicate that every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

It’s hard to abandon our grand looks and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

It has been revealed that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.
